fixes.explanation: That was Reuben's offer. He's another of Jacob's sons (Genesis 29:32), and on the first trip he offered his own two sons to his father if he didn't bring Simeon's brother back (Genesis 42:37). Judah's offer this time is different. He says, "You may hold me personally responsible."

Close to the money talk, but the man's warning wasn't about the price. Judah says it was about seeing his face again without their brother. The double silver comes up later, and it's Israel's idea, not the man's (Genesis 43:12). Israel is Jacob's other name, by the way (Genesis 35:10).

Right, Judah gives his father two options. Send their brother, and they'll go down and buy food. Don't send him, and he says, "…we will not go…" Then he repeats the man's warning right behind it. That's a man who wants to be heard.
Guards aren't part of Judah's offer. He says, "I will guarantee his safety." Then he tells his father, "You may hold me personally responsible." The promise is his own.

Judah says, "If we had not delayed, we could have come and gone twice by now." He's pointing out that all this waiting has cost them. It's like hitting snooze three times and then asking why the whole morning is gone. He's not wrong, though.
None of those are on Israel's list. He says to carry down "…a little balm and a little honey, spices and myrrh, pistachios and almonds." Wool, barley and dates aren't in it.

Israel says it just as written: "May God Almighty grant you mercy before the man, that he may release your other brother along with Benjamin." He says it to his sons. The other brother is the one kept back in Egypt (Genesis 42:24). I think a father sending his sons off with those words is doing what he can.

Israel says, "As for me, if I am bereaved, I am bereaved." I think he's bracing himself for the worst. Just before that he says, "May God Almighty grant you mercy before the man…" That's not an easy thing for a father to say out loud.

The text doesn't say he's sure. Israel says, "May God Almighty grant you mercy before the man…" That's a "may," a wish. Then he says, "…if I am bereaved, I am bereaved." I think that sounds like a man preparing himself for loss.

Israel is sending others. He tells his sons, "Take your brother as well, and return to the man at once." He says, "As for me, if I am bereaved, I am bereaved," before they leave. It's the men who hurry down to Egypt (Genesis 43:15).

Joseph, the man in charge in Egypt, tells his steward, "Take these men to my house. Slaughter an animal and prepare it, for they shall dine with me at noon." It's a dinner order. The brothers get frightened once they're taken to the house (Genesis 43:18).

That isn't his order. Joseph sees Benjamin with them and tells the steward to take them to his house and prepare a meal, "…for they shall dine with me at noon." Their first stop is his house, and lunch is set for noon.

Reuben is another of Jacob's sons (Genesis 29:32), but he's not the one the steward brings out. The text says the steward "…brought Simeon out to them." Simeon is the brother who was kept in Egypt (Genesis 42:24).
Levi is another of Jacob's sons (Genesis 29:34), but the text names Simeon here. The steward "…brought Simeon out to them." Simeon was the brother kept in Egypt (Genesis 42:24).
No laughing here. The text says Joseph "…was moved to tears for his brother, and he went to a private room to weep." I think this one hurts a little.

The text says, "…the Egyptians would not eat with the Hebrews, since that was detestable to them." So Joseph, his brothers and the Egyptians were each served separately. Same house, separate servings.
The text says they were seated in order by age, "…and the men looked at one another in astonishment." It doesn't say why. I'd be staring too if a seating chart got everybody's age right.

The text says, "…Benjamin’s portion was five times larger than any of the others." Five times, friend. If those portions were cookies, that's five on his side for every one on theirs. Then they all feasted and drank freely with Joseph.
Not even close. The text says, "…Benjamin’s portion was five times larger than any of the others." That's a big difference. Somebody at that table got a much bigger portion.
It goes the other way. Benjamin's portion "…was five times larger than any of the others." Not half the size. Five times the size.
